extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking stakeholders and commenters (regulated entities, NGOs, legal counsel, policymakers, and agency staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evidentiary standards the Administrator used to determine whether greenhouse gas air pollution may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or public welfare under the Clean Air Act, including how to interpret statutory terms, treat indirect effects, weigh sectoral evidence, and address uncertainties and adaptation. Intended to guide rulemaking findings and responses to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'well-being' and public welfare versus public health
rubrics_metrics.description: “The term well-being is a general term... would be to include effects on people that do not rise to the level of health effects. ... the much more logical way to interpret this provision ... is to interpret it as meaning effects on people other than health effects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give full meaning to both terms where Congress used different terms elsewhere; interpret well-being as effects on people other than health effects rather than as a partial subset of health effects. Do not read a textual basis that limits well-being to only indirect impacts or to only certain health effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of indirect health effects within public health endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may reasonably include health effects that occur because of climate change (indirect health effects) in its consideration of whether the air pollution endangers public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is overlap between public health and welfare, inclusion of indirect health effects in public health consideration is reasonable. Agency should evaluate indirect pathways (e.g., UV-B changes, injuries from secondary events) as relevant to public health rather than reclassifying them solely as welfare effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over chapter placement in assessing consistency with prior EPA documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of discussion in a 'welfare' chapter of a Criteria Document does not establish that EPA treats the underlying effects as welfare rather than health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating consistency with prior actions, examine how EPA staff evaluated the evidence and whether the agency treated the effects as health-relevant in policy assessments, rather than relying on where a discussion appears in a multi-chapter report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and proper reading of case law (NRDC, ATA) but distinguish applicable issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions prohibiting consideration of costs/feasibility in NAAQS rulemaking do not establish that EPA may not consider indirect health effects as public health issues for endangerment findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate the legal context (e.g., NAAQS standard-setting vs endangerment determinations). Do not overextend holdings about what considerations are permissible in one statutory provision to a different provision without analyzing the specific legal question addressed by the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on prospective mitigation or future controls to negate current endangerment
rubrics_metrics.description: “EPA is not considering the impacts of mitigation with respect to future reductions in emissions of greenhouse gases... For the same reasons, EPA is reasonably not considering mitigation in the form of the control measures that will need to be adopted in the future to reduce emissions of ozone precursors...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endangerment determinations should not be discounted because future mitigation or control programs exist or may be implemented; assess whether pollution is reasonably anticipated to endanger now and in the future regardless of speculative mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of adaptation in assessing health risk (heat vs cold balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize potential benefits of adaptation but do not presume adaptation will eliminate risk; consider literature indicating heat-related mortality is likely to increase and may exceed reductions in cold-related mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge adaptive measures and their potential to reduce mortality, but evaluate empirical projections and vulnerable populations. Where assessment literature shows increased frequency, magnitude, and duration of heat waves and growing vulnerable populations, adaptation does not negate an increased risk or endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of air-quality-mediated health impacts from climate change
rubrics_metrics.description: Air quality effects of climate change (e.g., increased ozone or PM) are relevant pathways by which climate change can endanger public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence that climate change will exacerbate ambient pollutant concentrations and therefore increase respiratory and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Consider these impacts in the endangerment finding rather than assuming other regulatory programs will eliminate the risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for timing and lags in NAAQS implementation when assessing interim health risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Controls to meet NAAQS are typically implemented after exceedances are detected and may take from three years to over twenty years to show effect; therefore interim increases in pollution can cause serious health impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume existing standards prevent all harm; consider the temporal gap between increased pollution and the deployment/effectiveness of controls when estimating health consequences of climate-related changes in pollutant levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of vulnerable individuals and evidence of no safe threshold for PM/ozone
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in attainment areas some at-risk individuals (e.g., with preexisting conditions) may experience health effects at levels below the standard; current evidence suggests there is no threshold for PM or ozone concentrations below which no effects can be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess impacts on sensitive subpopulations separately from population-level attainment metrics; recognize that standards offer a margin of safety but do not guarantee protection for all individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for exceptional events (e.g., wildfires) that escape normal CAA controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Some events, such as wildfires, may be 'exceptional events' not subject to standard NAAQS planning and controls but can produce emissions that adversely impact public health and are expected to increase due to climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include impacts from events that are not reasonably controllable or preventable under the usual regulatory process when evaluating overall public health endangerment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-by-sector assessment with a cross-sector weight-of-evidence judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator examined each climate-sensitive sector individually (food/agriculture; forestry; water resources; sea level/coastal areas; energy/infrastructure/settlements; ecosystems/wildlife) informed by scientific assessments and then viewed the full weight of evidence across sectors to decide endangerment to public welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct detailed sectoral analyses and then synthesize across sectors rather than relying on a single sector; weigh differing certainties, magnitudes, and directions of impact in forming an overall judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of impacts outside the U.S. and national security implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator considered impacts on the U.S. population from climate change effects occurring outside the United States, such as national security concerns that may arise as a result of impacts in other regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relevant, include transboundary and geopolitical/ national-security pathways by which foreign climate impacts can affect domestic welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agriculture — balance potential CO2/temperature benefits against adverse effects and interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elevated CO2 and modest temperature increases can stimulate some grain and oilseed yields in the near term, but benefits may be offset by enhanced pests/weeds/disease, higher temperatures, changing precipitation, and increased ground-level ozone; net effects are regionally variable and uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both beneficial and adverse mechanisms (CO2 fertilization, phenology changes, pests, weeds, disease, ozone, extreme events), consider near-term versus long-term trajectories, and explicitly account for offsetting factors and uncertainties when judging net impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agriculture — regional, crop-type, livestock, fisheries, and irrigation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different regions and crops (e.g., horticultural crops making up ~40% of crop value) have varying sensitivity; livestock production, irrigation needs, and fisheries will respond differently (cold-water fisheries likely harmed; warm-water fisheries may benefit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate agricultural impacts by commodity, region, and management system; include irrigation demand changes and vulnerabilities of horticultural crops where data are limited; treat fisheries by thermal affinity (cold/warm/cool-water species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestry — emphasize disturbances (wildfire, insects, drought) and regional productivity changes
rubrics_metrics.description: While CO2 and warmer temperatures may increase photosynthesis in some forests, increased frequency and size of wildfires, insect outbreaks, and droughts have very likely increased tree mortality and will continue to do so, causing significant adverse impacts in many regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize assessment of disturbance regimes and non-linear ecosystem changes (disturbance-driven shifts in structure/species) alongside incremental productivity effects; consider regional patterns (e.g., Interior West, Southwest, Alaska vs northeastern U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Water resources — assess quantity, timing, quality, recharge, salinization, and infrastructure resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate change alters the water cycle (shrinking snowpack, earlier melt, altered runoff timing, more intense precipitation and droughts), affects groundwater recharge, increases salinization in coastal areas, and exacerbates water quality problems (sediment, nutrients, pathogens, thermal pollution), stressing supplies and infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate hydrologic regime shifts (snowpack/runoff timing), regional variability in water availability, groundwater recharge changes, water quality deterioration, competing demands (agricultural/municipal/industrial/ecological), and vulnerability of treatment and management systems to extreme events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea level rise and coastal vulnerability — exposure, inundation, storm-surge, erosion, and wetland loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea level is rising along much of the U.S. coast and will likely increase, exacerbating progressive inundation, storm-surge flooding, shoreline erosion, and coastal wetland loss; population and infrastructure concentrations increase vulnerability in regions such as the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, Pacific Islands, and parts of Alaska.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess population and infrastructure exposure, regional differences, dynamic responses (coastal erosion, wetland squeeze), and ancillary impacts (e.g., saltwater intrusion of freshwater supplies); consider both present and projected future scenarios under higher-emission pathways.
